issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For physical abuse by a romantic partner, the threat profile is centered on generalized danger from strangers, while the appraisals are centered on bodily damage/shame and permanent emotional change. This is not impossible, but as the only represented components it is clinically hard to integrate into a single coherent profile of partner abuse without any partner-specific or trauma-linked threat content.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active links are between Negative Appraisals and Threat, so these two nodes should strongly cohere. Here the negative appraisals imply consequences focused on the body and self after intimate physical abuse, but the threat item 'threat from strangers approaching me' points to a different danger representation that is not reflected in the appraisals. That weakens the expected tight appraisal-threat coupling.

vignette:
Mele is an 80-year-old Tongan American woman who has been married for decades and still works as a welder, a point of pride she mentions early because it matters to her that people understand she has always been strong. When she speaks about the abuse, she does so plainly at first, almost as if describing a series of shop accidents, but the scenes are precise. The worst episodes happened at home with her husband, usually at night, when an argument would turn without warning and he would strike her hard enough to knock her against furniture or the floor. She remembers the shock of not knowing when the next blow was coming, the feeling of her body no longer being under her own control, and the long moments afterward lying awake and listening for movement in the house. What remains vivid for her is not only the pain itself but the sense that nowhere indoors was truly safe, not even the bedroom, not even behind a locked door. In her mind, the danger had come from the person beside her in the place that was supposed to protect her.

In the months and years afterward, Mele did not describe herself as frightened so much as changed. She had come to believe that what happened had permanently damaged her body. She talks about her body now as if it were something untrustworthy, something that can fail her without warning. If she feels stiffness, a sudden ache, or a moment of weakness after a long day, her mind goes quickly to the abuse and to the idea that she was injured in some lasting way. She is certain that her body is no longer reliable in the way it once was. Even routine sensations can unsettle her because they seem to confirm that she cannot depend on herself physically. She does not offer elaborate explanations; rather, she returns again and again to the same conviction: "Something in me got ruined." Alongside this is a quieter grief. She says she no longer feels normal emotions. Around family she can act appropriately, and at work she can be practical and composed, but inside she experiences herself as flattened, cut off from the ordinary warmth or ease she remembers from earlier life. What frightens her most is the thought that this is final, that whatever part of her used to feel fully alive has gone for good.

Her nights show most clearly how present the threat still feels. Sleep has become fractured and effortful. She has trouble falling asleep because once the house is quiet she begins listening. If she does drift off, she wakes suddenly and fully alert, often sitting up at once to check whether she is safe. She listens for footsteps, doors, changes in the air of the house. Sometimes she gets out of bed to look down the hallway or check the locks, not because she thinks through a specific likelihood each time, but because remaining still feels impossible until she has confirmed her surroundings. Even inside her own home she stays on guard. She notices where sounds are coming from, whether someone is moving in another room, whether there is enough light to see. Home does not register in her body as a place where she can let down.

This same vigilance appears in smaller ways during her work as a welder. In the shop, sudden noise, vibration, and the need to remain physically steady all draw her attention back to her body. When she feels soreness in her arms or back after handling equipment, she does not dismiss it as ordinary strain. Instead she becomes preoccupied with whether her body is giving out, whether the old injuries have left damage that can no longer be contained by toughness or skill. She still completes her tasks, but coworkers have noticed that she startles awake during breaks if she dozes and that she prefers to position herself where she can see the entrance. She has not described this to them in psychological terms. To Mele, it is simply common sense to remain prepared.

At home, the accumulation has been harder on her marriage and daily life than she first allowed herself to admit. The nightly checking means neither she nor her husband sleeps normally. She stays tense in bed, alert to movement, and the house has come to feel more like territory to monitor than a place to rest. During the day she moves through routines dutifully, but with little expectation of comfort. She sought help only recently, after recognizing that the pattern was not easing with time and that age had made her more aware of how much energy it takes to live this way. She says she came because she wants "one full night of sleep" and because she would like, before the end of her life, to know whether it is possible to feel like herself again. At the same time, she is afraid of being told that her fears are true: that her body has been permanently damaged, that she can never trust it again, and that the numbness she now calls normal will be all that is left.
